headline: Senate bill that would have required photo ID to vote in federal elections did not advance on August 8, 2026.
what_it_does: The bill would have barred election officials from giving a ballot in a federal election to anyone who does not show valid physical photo ID. People without ID could cast a provisional ballot, but it would count only if they showed ID, or signed a statement saying they have a religious objection to being photographed, within three days. Voters using methods other than in-person voting, such as mail ballots, would have had to include a copy of their photo ID, or the last four digits of their Social Security number plus a signed statement that they could not get a copy after reasonable efforts.

who_it_affects.how: They would have had to show valid physical photo ID to get a ballot at the polls.
They could cast a provisional ballot that would count only if they returned with ID or a religious-objection statement within three days.

who_it_affects.group: People who vote by mail or other non-in-person methods
who_it_affects.how: They would have had to send a copy of their photo ID, or the last four digits of their Social Security number with a signed statement, along with their ballot.

who_it_affects.group: Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters
who_it_affects.how: They would have been exempt from the ID rules for voting by methods other than in person.
They would have had to enforce the ID rules and, where practical, provide public devices for people to make free copies of their photo ID.
